sections.what: Brings in the Sentry tool and defines the four log levels: debug, info, warn, and error.
sections.why: Levels let the app mark how serious each message is.
sections.watch_out: Adding a new level means updating both this list and the logging rules.

sections.title: Shape of a log message

sections.why: Gives every log call the same structure.
sections.watch_out: Context is free-form, so the caller decides what goes into it.

sections.name: Logger, logger
sections.title: Logging rules and public methods
sections.what: Prints messages to the console according to the environment, and sends warnings and errors to Sentry in production. The public methods debug, info, warn, and error all pass through this one rule set.
sections.why: Keeps the console clean in production while making sure real problems are captured.
sections.watch_out: Debug and info messages never reach Sentry, so a problem described only by those levels will not show up there.

summary: A small logging helper for the web app that prints messages to the browser console and sends warnings and errors to Sentry when the app is live.
purpose: Gives the app one consistent way to record messages, instead of writing directly to the console. In production it keeps the console quiet and sends important problems to Sentry.
why: The file header calls this a standardized logger with Sentry integration. Keeping production quiet and sending only important events is likely to reduce noise and cost.
how: Each call (debug, info, warn, error) adds a timestamp and the level. In development every message goes to the console. In production only errors go to the console. Warnings and errors are also sent to Sentry, with extra context attached when it is provided.
inputs: A message text, an optional error object, and optional context details such as ids or page names.
outputs: Console lines in development, and Sentry events in production.
risks: Context details are sent to Sentry, so any health data placed in context would leave the browser. Non-error values passed as errors are sent as plain messages and lose their details. Debug and info messages are not sent to Sentry at all.
debug: If a problem does not appear in Sentry, check the environment is set to production and that the call used warn or error. If the console is noisy in production, check the level used. If context looks missing in Sentry, check that it is an object.
